outline.topic: The Logic of Light: A Calculus-Based Proof of Snell's Law
outline.target_audience: University students or advanced high school students with a basic understanding of calculus and optics.

sections.title: The Refraction Mystery
sections.content: Introduce the phenomenon of refraction where light bends at the interface of two media. Define the goal: to prove why light follows a specific path using Fermat's Principle of Least Time. Visually present the transition of a light ray from Air (Medium 1) to Water (Medium 2).
sections.example: A visual of a 'Laser Cat' pointing a laser into a fish tank, showing the beam visibly 'breaking' or bending as it hits the water surface.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Fermat’s Principle
sections.content: Establish the foundational rule: Light always takes the path that requires the least amount of time. Explain that because the speed of light (v) varies in different media (v = c/n), the straight-line distance is not always the fastest route.
sections.example: A split-screen animation showing a 'Lifeguard' running on sand (fast) and swimming in water (slow). To reach a drowning swimmer, the lifeguard doesn't run in a straight line; they run further on sand to minimize the time spent in the water.

sections.title: Setting Up the Geometric Model
sections.content: Create a coordinate system. Point A is at (0, a) in Medium 1. Point B is at (w, -b) in Medium 2. The light hits the interface at point (x, 0). Express the distances d1 (hypotenuse in Medium 1) and d2 (hypotenuse in Medium 2) using the Pythagorean theorem in terms of x.
sections.example: A clear geometric diagram showing two triangles. d1 = sqrt(x² + a²) and d2 = sqrt((w-x)² + b²), with angles θ1 and θ2 labeled relative to the normal line.

sections.title: The Time Function
sections.content: Formulate the total travel time T(x) as the sum of time spent in both media: T = (d1/v1) + (d2/v2). Substitute the distance expressions into the equation to create a single-variable function T(x).
sections.example: An overlay of the mathematical formula: T(x) = [sqrt(x² + a²) / v1] + [sqrt((w-x)² + b²) / v2]. Highlight the variable 'x' as the point that light 'chooses' to minimize time.

sections.title: Optimization via Calculus
sections.content: To find the minimum time, take the derivative of T with respect to x and set it to zero (dT/dx = 0). Show the step-by-step differentiation of the square root terms, resulting in x / (v1 * d1) - (w-x) / (v2 * d2) = 0.
sections.example: An animated sliding point 'x' on the boundary. As 'x' moves, a graph of T(x) above it shifts, showing the 'dip' where the derivative is zero.

sections.title: Connecting Geometry to Trigonometry
sections.content: Identify that x/d1 is exactly sin(θ1) and (w-x)/d2 is exactly sin(θ2) based on the triangles from Section 3. Substitute these into the derivative equation to get sin(θ1)/v1 = sin(θ2)/v2.
sections.example: The geometric diagram from earlier pulses the 'opposite' side and 'hypotenuse' of the triangles to visually link the ratio to the sine function.

sections.title: The Final Arrival: Snell’s Law
sections.content: Replace the velocities (v) with the refractive index formula (v = c/n). Show how (sin(θ1) / (c/n1)) = (sin(θ2) / (c/n2)) simplifies to the final form: n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2).
sections.example: A 'Formula Forge' animation where the variables clink together and simplify into the golden equation: n1 sinθ1 = n2 sinθ2, surrounded by a glowing aura of success.
